## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no evidence yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any success at all is a real signal. Two problems seem likely. (1) Recipe: the default recipe gives only 32 PPO updates (131k steps ÷ 4096 per update), which is very few. (2) Architecture: a brick lands at the highest point under its footprint, so a good placement needs every footprint cell at that landing layer to be missing from the build, without sealing missing cells below. A purely 2D network that flattens the layers has to rebuild layer-specific checks after pooling, which is hard. My plan is a near-factorial test: a per-layer network that shares weights across layers (A), the starting network with a recipe that gives more updates (B), and the per-layer network with a second recipe (C). B against A separates the network effect from the recipe effect, and A against C shows how much the recipe matters.

### Round 2
All four results so far are 0.000 on dev, and training success is also 0. These were the baseline net and a per-layer gated net, run at 4, 3 and 2 PPO epochs with 147k to 211k environment steps. Fewer epochs, more updates and more samples did not move anything off zero. The per-layer inductive bias on its own did not help either. An exact build needs every placement correct, no sealed holes, and DONE at the right moment, so the policy has to be very precise. That probably needs many more samples than we have used, a longer horizon to value the +1 bonus and avoid sealing, or both. Next steps: push sample volume to the limit with 1 epoch (about 426k steps); test gamma 0.99 so the agent cares about the terminal bonus and about cells it would seal later; and give the per-layer net features that summarise the column above and below each layer, for landing and sealing. All three use 1 epoch so they can be compared directly.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and also 0 training success in the last 10% of training. That held across two architectures, 1 to 3 PPO epochs, 147k to 405k steps and gamma 0.95 or 0.99. Seed noise cannot explain this. Even a rough greedy filler should sometimes build the smallest 6-brick designs exactly, so the agents are probably not learning the basic placement mapping at all. Every network so far assumes that the action logit at cell (y,x) of type t lines up spatially with the brick's top-left corner. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. If the action indexing is transposed, flipped or offset, a convolutional head that is aligned with the grid cannot express the policy, whatever the recipe. This round tests that guess with action heads that make no layout assumption: a CNN trunk with a fully connected (dense) action head, and a plain MLP. A third run tests the recipe on the baseline (no entropy bonus, longer horizon).

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, and this held across many different setups. Aligned conv heads, per-layer gated heads, a dense remap head and a flat MLP all failed. So did recipes with 1 to 3 epochs, 147k to 405k steps, gamma 0.95 or 0.99, and entropy 0. Because training success was also 0, the problem is not generalisation: the agent never learns to build any target exactly. Two explanations remain. First, the world may differ from its description, for example in action layout (flipped or transposed anchors, or position-major ordering). The dense and MLP heads could in principle learn any layout, but they may have learned too slowly. Second, too few policy-improvement iterations: the most any trial got was about 108 updates. For the last round I test both: a head that sums several plausible action layouts, and a recipe with about 400 small updates. Together with r3c3 (baseline net, 2 epochs, same as the second candidate's recipe), these form a 2x2 comparison.
